title: Book 12 — The Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, the cattle of the sun
paragraphs: “After we cleared the river Oceanus and reached the open sea, we sailed until we came to Aeaea, the island where dawn and sunrise occur just as they do everywhere else. We beached our ship on the sand and climbed out onto the shore, where we slept and waited for daybreak.

“When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, I sent some men to Circe’s house to retrieve Elpenor’s body. We gathered firewood from where the headland jutted into the sea, and after we had wept and mourned for him, we performed his funeral rites. Once his body and armor had been burned to ashes, we built a cairn, set a stone on it, and at the top of the cairn we planted the oar he had used for rowing.

“While we were busy with all this, Circe—who knew we had returned from the house of Hades—dressed herself and came to us as quickly as she could. Her maidservants came with her, bringing bread, meat, and wine. She stood among us and said, ‘You have accomplished something bold by going down alive to the house of Hades. You will have died twice while others die only once. Now stay here for the rest of the day, eat your fill, and continue your voyage at dawn tomorrow. Meanwhile, I will tell Odysseus about your route and explain everything to him, so that you don’t run into trouble, either by land or sea.’

“We agreed to do as she suggested and feasted all day until sunset. When the sun went down and darkness fell, the men lay down to sleep beside the ship’s stern cables. Then Circe took me by the hand and had me sit apart from the others. She reclined beside me and asked about all our adventures.

“‘So far, so good,’ she said when I had finished my story, ‘and now pay attention to what I am about to tell you—heaven itself will help you remember it. First you will come to the Sirens, who enchant everyone who comes near them. If anyone carelessly draws too close and hears the Sirens singing, his wife and children will never welcome him home again, for they sit in a green field and sing him to death with the sweetness of their song. There is a great heap of dead men’s bones lying all around, with the flesh still rotting off them. So sail past these Sirens, and stop your men’s ears with wax so that none of them can hear; but if you like, you may listen yourself, for you can have the men bind you upright on the crosspiece halfway up the mast, and they must lash the rope’s ends to the mast itself, so that you may have the pleasure of listening. If you beg and plead with them to set you free, they must bind you tighter still.

“‘When your crew have taken you past the Sirens, I cannot give you clear directions as to which of two courses you should take; I will lay the two before you, and you must consider them for yourself. On one side there are overhanging rocks against which the deep blue waves of Amphitrite beat with terrible fury; the blessed gods call these rocks the Wanderers. Not even a bird may pass that way, not even the timid doves that carry ambrosia to Father Zeus—the sheer rock always carries off one of them, and Father Zeus must send another to keep their number up. No ship that has ever come to these rocks has gotten away again; the waves and fiery whirlwinds carry off wreckage and the bodies of dead men. The only vessel that ever sailed through and survived was the famous Argo, on her way from the house of Aetes, and even she would have been dashed against these great rocks, had Hera not piloted her past them for love of Jason.

“‘Of these two rocks, one reaches to heaven and its peak is lost in a dark cloud that never leaves it, so that the top is never clear, not even in summer and early autumn. No man, though he had twenty hands and twenty feet, could get a foothold on it and climb it, for it rises sheer, as smooth as if it had been polished. Halfway up it there is a large cave, facing west and turned toward Erebus; you must take your ship this way, but the cave is so high up that not even the strongest archer could send an arrow into it. Inside it Scylla sits and yelps in a voice you might take for that of a young hound, but in truth she is a dreadful monster, and no one—not even a god—could face her without terror. She has twelve misshapen feet and six necks of enormous length, and at the end of each neck a frightful head with three rows of teeth, set close together, that could crunch anyone to death in a moment. She sits deep within her shadowy den, thrusting out her heads and peering all around the rock, fishing for dolphins or dogfish or any larger creature she can catch, out of the thousands that Amphitrite teems with. No ship has ever yet gotten past her without losing men, for she shoots out all her heads at once and carries off a man in each mouth.

“‘You will find the other rock lower, but they are so close together that there is not more than a bowshot between them. A large fig tree in full leaf grows on it, and beneath it lies the sucking whirlpool of Charybdis. Three times a day she spits her waters out, and three times she sucks them down again. See that you are not there when she is sucking them down, for if you are, not even Poseidon could save you. You must hug Scylla’s side and drive your ship past as fast as you can, for it is better to lose six men than your whole crew.’
“‘Is there no way,’ I said, ‘of escaping Charybdis, and at the same time keeping Scylla from harming my men?’

“‘You daredevil,’ replied the goddess, ‘you are always wanting to fight somebody or something; you will not let yourself be beaten even by the immortals. Scylla is not mortal—she is savage, fierce, wild, cruel, and invincible. There is no help for it; your best chance is to get past her as fast as you can, for if you linger by her rock while you are putting on your armor, she may strike again with her six heads and carry off another half dozen of your men. So drive your ship past her at full speed, and shout aloud to Crataiis, who is Scylla’s mother—curse her—and she will keep Scylla from making a second attack on you.’

“‘Next you will come to the Thrinacian island, and there you will find many herds of cattle and flocks of sheep belonging to the sun-god—seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep, with fifty head in each flock. They do not breed, and their numbers never grow fewer, and they are tended by the goddesses Phaethusa and Lampetie, who are children of the sun-god Hyperion by Neaera. Their mother, once she had borne them and finished nursing them, sent them off to the Thrinacian island, far away, to live there and watch over their father’s flocks and herds. If you leave these animals unharmed and think of nothing but getting home, you may yet reach Ithaca after much hardship; but if you harm them, then I warn you now of the destruction of both your ship and your comrades, and even if you yourself escape, you will come home late, in wretched condition, having lost all your men.’

“Here she ended, and Dawn, enthroned in gold, began to show in heaven, whereon she returned inland. I then went aboard and told my men to loose the ship from her moorings; so they got in at once, took their places, and began to strike the gray sea with their oars. Presently the great and clever goddess Circe sent us a fair wind that blew steady from astern and stayed with us, keeping our sails well filled, so we saw to whatever needed doing with the ship’s gear and let her go as wind and helmsman guided her.

“Then, deeply troubled, I said to my men, ‘My friends, it is not right that only one or two of us should know the prophecies Circe has given me; I will tell you about them, so that whether we live or die, we may do so with our eyes open. First she said we must keep clear of the Sirens, who sit and sing most beautifully in a field of flowers; but she said I might listen to them myself, so long as no one else did. So take me and bind me to the crosspiece halfway up the mast; bind me standing upright, with a bond so tight that I cannot possibly break free, and lash the rope’s ends to the mast itself. If I beg and plead with you to set me free, then bind me tighter still.’

“I had barely finished telling the men everything before we reached the island of the two Sirens, for the wind had been very favorable. Then, all of a sudden, it fell dead calm; there was not a breath of wind nor a ripple on the water, so the men furled the sails and stowed them; then, taking to their oars, they whitened the water with the foam they raised in rowing. Meanwhile I took a large wheel of wax and cut it up small with my sword. Then I kneaded the wax in my strong hands until it grew soft, which it soon did between the kneading and the rays of the sun-god, son of Hyperion. Then I stopped the ears of all my men, and they bound me hand and foot to the mast as I stood upright on the crosspiece, and went on rowing themselves. When we had come within earshot of the land, and the ship was moving at a good speed, the Sirens saw we were nearing the shore and began their song.

“‘Come here,’ they sang, ‘renowned Odysseus, honor to the Achaean name, and listen to our two voices. No one has ever sailed past us without staying to hear the enchanting sweetness of our song—and whoever listens goes on his way not only delighted but wiser, for we know all the sufferings the gods laid on the Argives and Trojans before Troy, and can tell you everything that is going to happen over the whole world.’

“They sang these words most musically, and as I longed to hear more of them, I made signs by frowning to my men that they should set me free; but they only rowed harder, and Eurylochus and Perimedes bound me with still tighter bonds until we had passed out of hearing of the Sirens’ voices. Then my men took the wax from their ears and untied me.

“Immediately after we had passed the island, I saw a great wave with spray rising from it, and I heard a loud roaring sound. The men were so frightened that they let go of their oars, for the whole sea resounded with the rush of the waters, but the ship stayed where it was, since the men had stopped rowing. I went around, therefore, and urged each man in turn not to lose heart.

“‘My friends,’ I said, ‘this is not the first time we have been in danger, and we are in nothing like so bad a case as when the Cyclops shut us up in his cave; even so, my courage and good counsel saved us then, and we shall live to look back on this too. Now, then, let us all do as I say—trust in Zeus and row on with might and main. As for you, helmsman, these are your orders: pay attention, for the ship is in your hands. Turn her head away from these boiling rapids and hug the rock, or she will slip away from you and you’ll find yourself over there before you know it, and you will be the death of us all.’

“So they did as I told them; but I said nothing about the terrible monster Scylla, for I knew the men would stop rowing if I did, and would huddle together in the hold. In one thing only did I disobey Circe’s strict instructions—I put on my armor. Then, taking two strong spears, I took my stand on the ship’s bow, since it was there I expected to first catch sight of the monster of the rock who was to do my men such harm; but I could not make her out anywhere, though I strained my eyes searching the gloomy rock over and over.

“Then we entered the Straits in great fear, for on one side was Scylla, and on the other dread Charybdis kept sucking up the salt water. As she vomited it up, it was like water boiling in a cauldron over a great fire, and the spray reached the tops of the rocks on either side. When she began to suck again, we could see the water inside whirling round and round, and it made a deafening sound as it broke against the rocks. We could see the bottom of the whirlpool, black with sand and mud, and the men were at their wits’ end with fear. While we were taken up with this, expecting each moment to be our last, Scylla suddenly swooped down upon us and snatched up my six best men. I was watching both ship and men at once, and in a moment I saw their hands and feet high above me, struggling in the air as Scylla carried them off, and I heard them call out my name in one last, despairing cry. As a fisherman, seated with his spear in hand on some jutting rock, throws bait into the water to deceive the poor little fish, and spears them with the ox-horn tip of his spear, throwing them gasping onto the land as he catches them one by one—even so did Scylla lift these struggling men up to her rock and devour them at the mouth of her den, while they screamed and stretched out their hands to me in their mortal agony. This was the most sickening sight I saw in all my voyages.

“When we had passed the Wandering rocks, with Scylla and terrible Charybdis, we reached the noble island of the sun-god, where were the fine cattle and sheep belonging to the sun Hyperion. While still at sea in my ship, I could hear the cattle lowing as they came home to their yards, and the sheep bleating. Then I remembered what the blind Theban prophet Tiresias had told me, and how carefully Aeaean Circe had warned me to shun the island of the blessed sun-god. So, being much troubled, I said to the men, ‘My men, I know you are hard pressed, but listen while I tell you the prophecy Tiresias made me, and how carefully Aeaean Circe warned me to shun the island of the blessed sun-god, for it was here, she said, that our worst danger would lie. Steer the ship, therefore, away from the island.’

“The men were dismayed at this, and Eurylochus at once gave me an insolent answer. ‘Odysseus,’ said he, ‘you are hard; you are very strong yourself and never wear out; you seem to be made of iron, and now, though your men are worn out with toil and lack of sleep, you will not let them land and cook themselves a good supper on this island, but tell them to put out to sea and go on faring fruitlessly through the watches of the swift night. It is by night that the winds blow hardest and do the most damage; how can we escape if one of those sudden squalls springs up from southwest or west, which so often wreck a ship when the gods, our masters, are unfavorable? Now, then, let us obey the demands of night and prepare our supper here beside the ship; tomorrow morning we will go aboard again and put out to sea.’

“Thus spoke Eurylochus, and the men agreed with him. I saw that heaven meant us harm, and said, ‘You force me to give way, since you are many against one, but each one of you must swear a solemn oath that if he comes upon a herd of cattle or a large flock of sheep, he will not be mad enough to kill a single head of either, but will be satisfied with the food Circe has given us.’

“They all swore as I told them, and when they had finished their oath we made the ship fast in a harbor near a stream of fresh water, and the men went ashore and cooked their suppers. As soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, they began talking about their poor comrades whom Scylla had snatched up and eaten; this set them weeping, and they went on crying until they fell into a sound sleep.

“In the third watch of the night, when the stars had shifted their places, Zeus raised a great gale of wind that blew like a hurricane, so that land and sea were covered with thick clouds, and night sprang forth out of the heavens. When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, we brought the ship to land and drew her into a cave where the sea-nymphs hold their courts and dances, and I called the men together in council.

“‘My friends,’ I said, ‘we have meat and drink in the ship, so let us take care not to touch the cattle, or we shall suffer for it, for these cattle and sheep belong to the mighty sun, who sees and hears everything.’ And again they promised that they would obey.

“For a whole month the wind blew steadily from the south, and there was no other wind but south and east. As long as the corn and wine held out, the men did not touch the cattle, hungry as they were; but when they had eaten everything there was in the ship, they were forced to range farther afield, with hook and line, catching birds and taking whatever they could lay their hands on, for they were starving. One day, therefore, I went up inland to pray to heaven to show me some way of escape. When I had gone far enough to be clear of all my men, and had found a place well sheltered from the wind, I washed my hands and prayed to all the gods on Olympus, until by and by they sent me off into a sweet sleep.

“Meanwhile Eurylochus had been giving the men evil counsel. ‘Listen to me,’ said he, ‘my poor comrades. All deaths are bad enough, but there is none so bad as death by famine. Why shouldn’t we drive in the best of these cows and offer them in sacrifice to the immortal gods? If we ever get back to Ithaca, we can build a fine temple to the sun-god and fill it with every kind of ornament; but if he is determined to sink our ship in revenge for these horned cattle, and the other gods agree with him, I for one would rather drink salt water once and be done with it than starve slowly to death on a desert island like this.’

“Thus spoke Eurylochus, and the men agreed with him. Now the cattle, so fair and fine, were feeding not far from the ship; the men, therefore, drove in the best of them, and they all stood around them saying their prayers, using young oak shoots instead of barley meal, since there was no barley left. When they had finished praying, they killed the cows and dressed the carcasses; they cut out the thigh bones, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and laid pieces of raw meat on top. They had no wine to pour as drink offerings over the sacrifice while it cooked, so they kept pouring a little water instead while the inner meats were grilling; then, when the thigh bones were burned and they had tasted the inner meats, they cut up the rest small and put the pieces on spits.

“By this time my deep sleep had left me, and I turned back toward the ship and the seashore. As I drew near, I began to smell hot roast meat, and groaned out a prayer to the immortal gods. ‘Father Zeus,’ I cried, ‘and all you other gods who live in everlasting bliss, you have done me a cruel mischief with the sleep you sent me; see what fine work these men of mine have made in my absence!’

“Meanwhile Lampetie went straight to the sun and told him we had been killing his cows, at which he flew into a great rage and said to the immortals, ‘Father Zeus, and all you other gods who live in everlasting bliss, I must have vengeance on the crew of Odysseus’s ship: they have had the insolence to kill my cows, which were the one thing I loved to look upon, whether I was going up to heaven or coming down again. If they do not make amends to me for my cows, I will go down to Hades and shine there among the dead.’
“‘Sun,’ said Zeus, ‘go on shining upon us gods and upon mankind over the fruitful earth. I will shatter their ship into little pieces with a bolt of white lightning as soon as they put out to sea.’
“I was told all this by Calypso, who said she had heard it from the mouth of Hermes.

“As soon as I got down to my ship and the seashore, I rebuked each of the men separately, but we could see no way out of it, for the cows were dead already. And indeed the gods soon began to show signs and wonders among us, for the hides of the cattle crawled about, and the meat on the spits began to low like cows, and the flesh, whether cooked or raw, kept making a noise just as cows do.

“For six days my men kept driving in the best cows and feasting on them, but when Zeus, son of Cronus, had added a seventh day, the fury of the gale died down; so we went aboard, raised the mast, spread sail, and put out to sea. As soon as we were well away from the island, and could see nothing but sky and sea, the son of Cronus raised a black cloud over our ship, and the sea grew dark beneath it. We had not gone much further when we were caught by a fierce squall from the west that snapped the forestays of the mast, so that it fell backward, while all the ship’s gear tumbled about at the bottom of the vessel. The mast struck the helmsman on the head as it fell, crushing his skull to pieces, and he fell overboard as though he were diving, with no more life left in him.

“Then Zeus let fly with his thunderbolts, and the ship spun round and round and was filled with fire and brimstone as the lightning struck it. The men all fell into the sea; they were carried about in the water round the ship, looking like so many sea-gulls, but the god soon deprived them of any chance of getting home again.

“I clung to the ship until the sea knocked her sides away from her keel, which drifted off by itself, and tore the mast out of her in the direction of the keel; but there was a backstay of stout ox-hide still fastened to it, and with this I lashed the mast and keel together, and getting astride of them, I was carried wherever the winds chose to take me.

“The gale from the west had by now spent its force, and the wind shifted back into the south, which frightened me, for I feared I would be carried back to the terrible whirlpool of Charybdis. And that is just what happened: I was borne along by the waves all night, and by sunrise had reached the rock of Scylla and the whirlpool. She was then sucking down the salt sea water, but I was carried up toward the fig tree, which I caught hold of and clung to like a bat. I could not plant my feet anywhere to stand securely, for the roots were far below and the boughs that overshadowed the whole pool were too high, too vast, and too far apart for me to reach; so I hung on patiently, waiting for the pool to discharge my mast and raft again—and it seemed a very long while. A juror is no more glad to get home to supper, after being long detained in court by troublesome cases, than I was to see my raft beginning to work its way out of the whirlpool again. At last I let go with my hands and feet and fell heavily into the sea, close by my raft, climbed onto it, and began to row with my hands. As for Scylla, the father of gods and men would not let her catch sight of me again—otherwise I would certainly have been lost.

“From there I was carried along for nine days, until on the tenth night the gods brought me ashore on the Ogygian island, where the great and powerful goddess Calypso lives. She took me in and was kind to me, but I need say no more about this, for I told you and your noble wife all about it yesterday, and I hate telling the same story over and over again.”
